subject: AI & Agents
title: Naive Bayes: Probability to the Rescue
description: A fast breakdown of Naive Bayes: Probability to the Rescue for builders.

hook.text: An email contains 'winner,' 'prize,' and 'click here.' What's the probability it's spam? Very high.

buildup.text: Naive Bayes uses Bayes' theorem to calculate the probability of each class given the evidence.

discovery.text: It's 'naive' because it assumes features are independent — which is usually wrong but works anyway.

twist.text: Despite the wrong assumption, it often beats more complex models on text classification.

climax.text: Gmail's original spam filter was built on Naive Bayes. Simplicity won.

punchline.text: Wrong assumptions, right answers. Classic machine learning.

quiz.question: Why is Naive Bayes called 'naive'?
options: It assumes all features are independent of each other
It's too simple to be useful
It was the first algorithm invented

details.summary: Naive Bayes classifiers use probability theory to make predictions, assuming features are independent. Despite this naive assumption being usually wrong, the method works remarkably well for text classification.
details.whyItMatters: Naive Bayes powers spam filters and text classifiers with minimal computation. It demonstrates that simple models with wrong assumptions can still outperform complex ones when data is limited.
takeaways: Naive Bayes applies probability theory assuming feature independence
The independence assumption is wrong but the method still works well
It is fast, simple, and effective for text classification tasks

faq.question: Why is it called 'naive' if it works well?
faq.answer: It naively assumes all features are independent of each other, which is rarely true. The word 'free' and 'money' appearing together in spam are correlated, but Naive Bayes ignores this. It works despite the wrong assumption.

faq.question: Where is Naive Bayes commonly used?
faq.answer: Email spam filtering, sentiment analysis, document categorization, and medical diagnosis. It is especially popular when training data is limited because it needs fewer examples to learn than more complex algorithms.
